source.text:
An emergency fund has one job: be there, intact and reachable, on the day something goes wrong. That makes choosing where to keep it a slightly different exercise than chasing the biggest number on a rate table. For a $15,000 cushion, the three things that matter most are no monthly fees, federal deposit insurance, and transfers that move quickly when you need the cash. Yield matters too, but it comes fourth.

The good news is that the bar to clear is low. The FDIC puts the national average savings rate at just 0.38%, and basic savings accounts at big banks such as Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America still pay around 0.01%. On $15,000, that is the difference between pocket change and several hundred dollars a year at a competitive online bank. Every account below carries federal deposit insurance up to $250,000, so a $15,000 balance is fully covered at any of them.

Our top pick for most emergency savers this month is Varo. Varo was one of the first fintech companies to obtain a national bank charter, which lets it offer FDIC insurance and a fuller set of banking services directly. There are no monthly fees and no minimum deposit requirement, and you earn interest as long as you keep at least $0.01 in the account. Its 3.75% APY applies to your entire balance with no cap, so a full $15,000 emergency fund earns the headline rate. The one condition is that you need qualifying direct deposits totaling $1,000 or more each month, which most people with a regular paycheck clear without thinking about it. Because Varo also offers a checking account, your emergency money sits under the same roof as your everyday spending account.

If you would rather avoid monthly conditions altogether, Vio Bank is the strongest no-strings option. Its 4.00% APY applies to all balances with no required monthly activity and no monthly fees, though you will need $100 to open the account. The tradeoff is access: Vio, the online banking division of MidFirst Bank, has no checking account and no physical branches, so you have to transfer money to an external bank before you can spend it.

EverBank is the pick for people who want a bank with some physical footprint. It pays 3.90% APY with no minimum opening deposit, no monthly fees and no required monthly behavior, and its mobile app holds a 4.7-star rating on Google Play and the Apple App Store. Its branches are concentrated mostly in Florida, California and New York.

Axos Bank posts the biggest number on most rate tables: up to 4.21% APY through its ONE bundle. Earning it requires $1,500 in monthly direct deposits plus a $1,500 average daily balance in checking, or $5,000 in monthly deposits and a $5,000 average daily balance. Fall short in any month and the rate drops to a 1.00% base APY. For an emergency fund, money you may have to drain at an inconvenient moment, that cliff is a real risk.

LendingClub's LevelUp Savings works on a similar principle at a smaller scale. Deposit at least $250 in a statement cycle and you earn 4.00% on the entire balance; miss it and you earn 3.00%. It does include an ATM card with no ATM fees, which is unusual for an online savings account and handy if you ever need cash in a hurry.

Marcus by Goldman Sachs has long been a default recommendation, and it is still a clean product: no monthly fee, no minimum opening deposit, no minimum balance to earn its 3.50% APY, and customer service available around the clock. But it is a weaker fit for emergency money than its reputation suggests. Marcus does not offer same-day transfers; moving money out to an external checking account typically takes three to five business days. It also limits savings withdrawals to six per month and charges $10 for each one beyond that. With no checking account and no ATM access, there is no faster route to your cash when an emergency hits.

Ally remains a reasonable choice if you like organization tools. Its Buckets feature lets you label part of a single balance for emergencies, there is no monthly maintenance fee, and standard ACH transfers are free. Be aware that Ally charges $10 per excess withdrawal after six in a month and offers no branch or ATM access. Synchrony is another no-fee, no-minimum option at 3.40% APY, and it adds an optional ATM card that works at machines showing the Plus or Accel logo.

A few final rules of thumb. Every rate here is variable and can change at any time, so do not over-optimize for a few hundredths of a percent; a quarter-point difference on $15,000 is under $40 a year. Put speed of access ahead of yield, keep the account at a federally insured institution, and be wary of rates that hinge on keeping a balance you may need to spend down in exactly the month an emergency arrives.
